reason: The text does not present violence as a model for good leadership. The passage describes Moses, Joshua, and Caleb as faithful leaders who respond to the people's rebellion with prayer, intercession, and faithful speech rather than violence. When the congregation threatens to stone Joshua and Caleb (an act of violence), God intervenes to stop it. The righteous leaders exemplified here—Moses (who prays and intercedes), Caleb (who speaks truthfully with faith), and Joshua (who stands with Caleb)—are rewarded precisely because they do not resort to violence. God's punishment is divine judgment (the generation will die in the wilderness), not a model of violent leadership that Moses is commanded to implement. The narrative actually demonstrates that faithful, non-violent response to unrest is the leadership model being commended.
